verdict.rationale: GitHub's own docs say you can read and write repository data over SSH using key-based authentication. They also cover cloning with Git and adding remotes with standard `git remote add`, so the core clone/push workflow with a standard Git client is documented. Community reports of students running `push -u origin master` show ordinary Git pushes reaching GitHub; the rejection was about the branch name, not the protocol. Missing for 10: explicit documentation of the HTTPS transport, explicit coverage of pull/fetch operations.

support.subject: As a developer, I can clone, pull, and push repositories with any standard Git client over HTTPS or SSH

citations.quote: You can access and write data in repositories on GitHub using SSH (Secure Shell Protocol). When you connect via SSH, you authenticate using a private key file on your local machine.
you can add the public key to your account on GitHub.com to enable authentication for Git operations over SSH.
Clone a repository to your local computer using Git.
To add a new remote, use the `git remote add` command on the terminal, in the directory your repository is stored at.
